newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Oil giants queue for Venezuelan gasoline opening.
newsitem.headline: Oil giants queue for Venezuelan gasoline opening.

text.p: The world's oil multinationals are queuing up to take a slice of Venezuela's gasoline retail market if and when it opens to private capital in the next few months, industry sources said on Thursday.

The government's liberalisation proposal, which is currently being studied by Congress, could lead to 1,000 new stations being built in the country over the next four years, attracting a total $1 billion in new investment, they added.

International firms Royal Dutch/Shell, Mobil, Texaco, British Petroleum, Chevron, Amoco and Exxon are all rumoured to be interested in opening supply networks, while Repsol and YPF are waiting in the wings.

On the domestic front, state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) has created a new subsidiary, Deltaven, to compete in the 350,000 barrel per day market and a consortium of Venezuelan retailers, Trebolgas, is also hoping to get a piece of the cake.

PDVSA, which currently has a monopoly on gasoline wholesale, has said it would like to retain 40-50 percent of the market after liberalisation. But industry sources say it may struggle even to hold on to that given the scale of the competition.

About 90 percent of Venezuela's 1,600 service stations are privately-owned, so new market entrants will have to offer better wholesale contracts to existing owners. In addition, they will buy land, build new stations and rent them to independent operators.
Industry sources say average throughput at Venezuela's stations of 600,000 litres per month was double the Latin American average.
"I don't see scope for the addition of 2,000 new stations, but I would expect another 500 to 1,000 to be built within 3-4 years," said an international oil company executive in Venezuela.

The government currently pays 6.5 bolivars (1.3 cents) per litre as a retail margin to station operators and 2.5 bolivars (0.5 cents) per litre to truckers for delivery from depots to stations. PDVSA president Luis Giusti said recently the true cost of distributing gasoline was 16 bolivars per litre, and multinational companies say this might rise to about 20 bolivars per litre if one allows for a 10-15 percent return on investment.

"There is no huge rise in margins... 20 bolivars per litre is what is necessary in order to cover costs and investments in a market. Of course, it would be subject to market forces, but that would be an economic margin," an industry source said.

Gasoline prices, which are still controlled by the Energy and Mines Ministry, rose 27 percent on Thursday to 80 bolivars (16 cents) per litre for high octane, versus Giusti's estimated break-even cost of 83 bolivars (17 cents), including tax, royalties and distribution.

If the market is liberalised, prices would be capped by international markets because private companies would also be allowed to import, although they would be unlikely to achieve that level since Venezuela is a major gasoline exporter.
